cells.tense: You are standing in the clearing and the frame you build next is yours to draw.
cells.ask: Sketch the structure that replaced the old one, corners and all, before the shape softens. A real frame needs an edge.
cells.core:
Something came down and the ground is clear. You're the one holding the pen, and the structure you draw next lands because you'd say out loud that you're the one drawing it. When a frame serves what it organizes, things make sense in the room with you in it, and people feel that without being told.

The honest version isn't only openness. There's a lot you can see and not yet prove, and holding both is part of what keeps the frame standing. Sketch the new building today, edges first. Then watch one day with it and see what the shape holds, and what it doesn't.

cells.tense: You are bracing for the collapse still coming and drawing faster than the ground can hold.
cells.ask: Pick the one structure you're about to declare and leave it undesigned for a week. Write down what arrives without you.
cells.core:
There's a clearing ahead and you're trying to build in it before the dust settles. The replacement is sketched, defended, organized for — and the building isn't up yet, which makes you press harder. The clear structure you're reaching for is one you'd trust quietly, not one you'd keep convincing people to stand in.

The pushing spends the exact calm the new structure would run on. Let one announcement stay unsaid for a week. Write down what shows up in the space instead — the material's own shape, not yours. That's how the solid kind of frame gets built, and it's lighter than what you're carrying now.
cells.sheetLine: You're building the next thing before the ground is dry.

cells.tense: Something fell a while back and you are still standing where the old walls used to be.
cells.ask: Name one structure that's gone and say out loud that it's gone. Then start one small build that doesn't depend on it.
cells.core:
A structure came down and you haven't said so. You still describe the situation as if the old arrangement were load-bearing — the same job, the same part you played. From outside, what's true is that you walked through, and the clearing is what you'd find if you turned and looked at it.

A frame rises here. You have enough to say what's gone, and the not-saying is what keeps you at the closed door. Let one small deliberate thing get built today, one you'd choose on purpose. Doing it in the open is the way back into what's already yours.

cells.tense: You are clearing false structure while describing the week as something that just happened to you.
cells.ask: Go back to one thing you ended and count plainly what it gave you. Say out loud that you chose the ending.
cells.core:
Things have been coming down around you — plans, assumptions, the shape a week was supposed to have — and your account of it is passive. None of it was yours to make; these things just fall. But the clearing looks different depending on who's standing in it, and the ones who can use it are the ones who'd claim it.

Somewhere underneath there's a decision you made, and the ending was yours. Go back to one thing you ended and count what it grew, plainly, out loud. Then keep one piece. The credit is what makes the clearing useful next time it's yours.

The asks survive being wrong: sketching a frame, leaving one announcement undesigned, saying a fallen thing is gone, counting one ending — each teaches something about structure on its own.
